passage: The youth centre in Leeds held a pizza night every Friday, and Jamal went because his mum made him. He took the chair nearest the door, hood up, phone out even though there was no signal. Bilal and three others from his class were arguing about a football match a few metres away. Jamal knew the answer; he had watched the whole second half. He kept quiet. They don't want me in it anyway, he thought, and scrolled through nothing. Once Bilal glanced over. 'You alright, mate?' Jamal shrugged without looking up. Bilal turned back to the others. By half eight the group had drifted to the pool table, and Jamal sat alone with a cold slice. See, he told himself on the walk home. Nobody talks to me. He didn't think about the shrug.

qa.q: Where did Jamal sit at the pizza night?
qa.a: Jamal took the chair nearest the door, hood up, phone out even though there was no signal.

qa.q: What was Jamal thinking when he kept quiet about the football argument?
qa.a: He was thinking 'They don't want me in it anyway', so he expected to be unwelcome even though he knew the answer.

qa.q: At which moment could Jamal have changed how the night went, and how?
qa.a: When Bilal asked 'You alright, mate?', Jamal could have looked up and mentioned the second half he watched, which would have let him into the conversation.

qa.q: How might Bilal have read Jamal's hood, phone and shrug?
qa.a: To Bilal it probably looked as if Jamal wasn't interested in them, so leaving him alone seemed like the polite thing to do.

grounding: Shows a teenager who expects classmates to reject him acting withdrawn, so they leave him alone and he takes that as proof.

passage: Room 14 of the Class 10 boys' hostel had cake for Mridul's birthday at nine, after study hour. Eshaan came because the warden said everyone should. He stood by the window, arms folded, and checked his watch twice where people could see. Last term someone had laughed at his accent in the mess; since then he had been sure the whole floor thought he was odd. When the carrom board came out, Mridul held a striker toward him. 'Play one round?' 'I'm okay,' Eshaan said, and yawned, though he wasn't tired. Mridul passed the striker on. Later, walking to brush his teeth, Eshaan heard Mridul in the corridor: 'Leave him, yaar, he finds us boring.' Eshaan lay in his bunk, face hot. Knew it, he thought. They never wanted me there.

qa.q: What did Mridul offer Eshaan when the carrom board came out?
qa.a: Mridul held a striker toward him and asked, 'Play one round?'

qa.q: Why did Eshaan's face go hot in his bunk?
qa.a: He felt hurt, and he took Mridul's words as proof of what he had believed since last term, that the floor thought he was odd.

qa.q: What choice at the carrom board might have changed the night for Eshaan?
qa.a: Taking the striker for just one round would have shown the others he wanted to be there, instead of the folded arms and yawn they read as boredom.

qa.q: Why might Mridul have said 'he finds us boring'?
qa.a: From where Mridul stood, Eshaan checked his watch, yawned and turned down the game, so it honestly looked like Eshaan didn't want their company.

grounding: Illustrates how a boy's belief that his hostel mates dislike him leads to cold behaviour that makes them step back, which he reads as confirmation.

passage:
Dear Sangeeta akka,
You asked how the new school is. Same as I said. The girls here have known each other since KG and they don't want a new girl in the group.
Last Saturday there was a class picnic at the lake. I sat on the steps with my book and my earphones in. No music. I just didn't want anyone thinking I was waiting to be asked.
Two girls did come over and said the samosas were in the blue box. I said 'okay' and went back to reading. After that they didn't come again. On the bus home I sat alone.
Amma says I should 'make an effort'. What effort, when they've already decided?
Maybe I look like I don't care. I do care, a bit. Don't tell Amma that part.
Love,
Lakshmi

qa.q: What did the two girls tell Lakshmi at the picnic?
qa.a: They said the samosas were in the blue box.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi wear earphones with no music at the picnic?
qa.a: Lakshmi didn't want anyone thinking Lakshmi was waiting to be asked, which suggests a fear of looking hopeful and then being turned away.

qa.q: When the two girls came over, what could Lakshmi have done differently?
qa.a: Lakshmi could have taken the earphones out, thanked them and walked to the blue box with them, giving the conversation a chance to keep going.

qa.q: How might the two girls have felt after Lakshmi said 'okay' and went back to the book?
qa.a: They probably felt brushed off and decided Lakshmi preferred to be alone, which is why they didn't come again.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl who assumes the classmates don't want a newcomer, stays closed off at a picnic, and then sees their distance as proof.

passage: 'Talent.' That's what I used to call it. I'm Zeenat, I edited our college paper in final year, and two first-years joined the same week: Dilnaz and Ritwik. Dilnaz spoke up in the first meeting, so I gave her the hostel water story, a real investigation. Ritwik was quiet, so I gave him the events calendar. Just dates. By March, Dilnaz had interviewed the warden, rewritten her piece three times with my notes, and it was our most-read story. Ritwik was still doing the calendar, and in my head he'd become 'the calendar guy'. Then one night he sent me a draft nobody had asked for, about the canteen workers' shift timings. Rough, but sharp. I sat there and realised I had never once gone through edits with him the way I did with Dilnaz. I gave her my attention and him a list, and then called the difference talent.

qa.q: What task did Zeenat first give Ritwik?
qa.a: Zeenat gave him the events calendar. Just dates.

qa.q: What did Zeenat realise after reading Ritwik's canteen draft?
qa.a: Zeenat realised the gap between the two first-years came partly from Zeenat's own attention, since Dilnaz got edits and notes while Ritwik only got a list.

qa.q: What could Zeenat do now with Ritwik's draft, and why would it matter?
qa.a: Zeenat could go through edits on the canteen story with Ritwik, the same way as with Dilnaz, so he finally gets the feedback and chance she got.

qa.q: What might the months on the calendar have been like for Ritwik?
qa.a: He may have felt overlooked and unsure what he could do, which could explain why he wrote a story nobody asked for, to show he was capable of more.

grounding: A student editor notices that the junior given a real investigation grew while the one given only a calendar stalled, because attention and feedback followed expectations.

passage: I'm Chinmay. I've trained the new lads at our cycle workshop for two years, so I see how they grow. This summer we took Eshaan and Pratik, both nineteen. The owner liked Eshaan's chatter and handed him a full gear overhaul on day three. Pratik got punctures. Only punctures, for six weeks. When Eshaan got stuck on the derailleur, the owner stood next to him, pointing, explaining. By his next overhaul Eshaan worked alone, whistling. Pratik fixed punctures fast and clean, then stood around. Nobody checked his work because nobody thought it needed checking. By August he had stopped asking questions. I can't say what was going on in his head. Maybe boredom, maybe he'd decided that's all he was good for. Last week I gave him a brake job and stayed close. He took forty minutes and asked six questions.

qa.q: What job did Pratik get for six weeks?
qa.a: Pratik got punctures. Only punctures, for six weeks.

qa.q: What does Pratik asking six questions on the brake job suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests he still wanted to learn and came alive once someone trusted him with harder work and stayed close.

qa.q: Which choice by Chinmay could change Pratik's path, and why?
qa.a: Chinmay gave him a brake job and stayed close, giving Pratik the same mix of challenge and attention that helped Eshaan improve.

qa.q: What would change if the owner had handed Pratik the gear overhaul on day three?
qa.a: Pratik would probably have had someone beside him explaining, and he might have grown the way Eshaan did instead of stalling.

grounding: A young trainer observes that the junior trusted with hard work got attention and grew, while the one kept on simple tasks got little feedback and stagnated.

passage:
Monday, first week at the coaching centre: Sangeeta, twenty-two and newly made senior tutor, split the two new tutors. Gopika got the Class 12 physics batch. Harsha got attendance and photocopies. 'He's quiet,' she told the owner. 'Let him settle.'
Thursday, fourth week: Gopika's lecture on circuits lost half the room. Sangeeta sat at the back, then spent twenty minutes with her afterwards: slow down, use one example, ask questions. Gopika's next class was sharper. Harsha finished the photocopies by ten and scrolled his phone. Sangeeta didn't speak to him all day.
Saturday, eighth week: Gopika was drawing ray diagrams while students called out answers. In the staffroom Harsha asked, very quietly, 'Am I just not tutor material?' Sangeeta opened her mouth to reassure him and stopped. She had never watched him teach once. That evening she wrote his name next to the Class 9 batch, with a note: sit in on Tuesday.

qa.q: Which batch did Gopika get in the first week?
qa.a: Gopika got the Class 12 physics batch.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta stop before reassuring Harsha?
qa.a: She realised she had never watched him teach once, so she had no real basis for judging him and felt her own choices had held him back.

qa.q: What turning point did Sangeeta reach on Saturday, and what did she choose?
qa.a: Harsha's question made her see the gap, and she chose to give him the Class 9 batch and sit in on Tuesday to give him feedback.

qa.q: How might the eight weeks have looked from Harsha's side?
qa.a: Harsha only got photocopies and silence, so he may have started to believe he wasn't good enough, which is why he asked if he was tutor material.

grounding: A young senior tutor sees that the junior trusted with a hard batch got feedback and improved, while the one given simple chores got no attention and stagnated.

subtype: Predicting failure and drifting into it [Actor]
passage:
Subject: Interview, as predicted

Harish bhaiya,
It went exactly how I said it would. You kept telling me to prepare, but they were always going to pick someone from a big design school. So I looked at my portfolio once on Sunday and went to sleep at two anyway, because I couldn't stop thinking about it.
In the room my voice was shaking before I'd even sat down. They asked what I thought of their museum signage project. I hadn't looked at their website. I said something about 'clean fonts'. One of them wrote a note and didn't look up again.
'We'll let you know.' We both know what that means.
So there it is. I was right. You'll say I didn't prepare, and fine, I didn't, but what was the point if the result was fixed?
Tell Ma I'll call on the weekend.
Parul

qa.q: What did the panel ask Parul about?
qa.a: They asked what Parul thought of their museum signage project.

qa.q: How can you tell Parul was anxious before the interview even began?
qa.a: Parul went to sleep at two because the worry wouldn't stop, and Parul's voice was shaking before sitting down.

qa.q: What choice in the days before could have changed the outcome for Parul?
qa.a: Instead of looking at the portfolio once, Parul could have read up on the firm's work, including the museum signage project, and practised answers with Harish.

qa.q: How might Harish see Parul's line 'I was right'?
qa.a: Harish, who kept urging preparation, would likely see that Parul's belief in failure led to the thin preparation that caused the bad interview.

grounding: Shows a young adult so sure of failing an interview that they barely prepare, arrive shaky and do badly, then treat the result as proof.

subtype: Predicting failure and drifting into it [Actor]
passage: Madhuri, pass the sugar. Okay, so, the school interview. You know I'm Vandana, the girl who never gets past round two, right? So I didn't bother planning the demo lesson properly. Why spend three evenings on it? I watched that cooking show instead and told myself I'd 'wing it'. Morning of, my hands were so cold I had to hold my tea glass for five minutes. They gave me Class 6, fractions. I'd been thinking of doing pizzas on the board, but I hadn't drawn one before, and it came out like an egg. The kids laughed. Then the principal asked how I'd help a child who was falling behind, and my mind went white. I said 'extra worksheets'. That's it. Two words. And I thought, see, Vandana, this is what always happens. I'm just not an interview person. Why are you looking at me like that?

qa.q: Which class and topic did Vandana get for the demo lesson?
qa.a: They gave Vandana Class 6, fractions.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling on the morning of the interview, and what shows it?
qa.a: Vandana was very anxious, with hands so cold that holding the tea glass for five minutes was the only way to warm them.

qa.q: What would you advise Vandana before the next interview?
qa.a: Spend the evenings practising the demo lesson, including drawing it on a board, and prepare one or two real ideas for helping a child who falls behind.

qa.q: Why might Madhuri be looking at Vandana like that?
qa.a: Madhuri probably sees that Vandana chose not to prepare because of the fear, and that this, not bad luck, is why the interview went badly.

grounding: A young woman convinced of failing a teaching interview skips planning, arrives anxious and performs poorly, then takes it as confirmation.

subtype: Predicting failure and drifting into it [Actor]
passage: I'm Sabina, and I share a flat with Bhupen. The week before his bank interview, I kept offering to do mock questions with him. 'No point,' he said every time. 'They'll take someone with better marks.' He spent Wednesday rearranging his bookshelf. Thursday he played cricket videos till late. The night before, he ironed his shirt at one in the morning and kept saying, 'It's already gone, I can feel it.' I can't know exactly what was in his head. I only know he left without breakfast and his tie was crooked. He came back at noon and dropped onto the sofa. 'They asked about current rates and I blanked,' he said. 'Told you. I knew it.' He looked almost relieved, like being right was the one good thing about the day. I wanted to say he never gave himself a chance, but I just made him tea.

qa.q: What did Bhupen spend Wednesday doing?
qa.a: He spent Wednesday rearranging his bookshelf.

qa.q: Why might Bhupen have looked almost relieved after the interview?
qa.a: He had been so sure it would go badly that being proved right felt like the one good thing, a kind of comfort in the fear coming true.

qa.q: What could Bhupen have done differently when Sabina offered mock questions?
qa.a: He could have accepted the mock questions and prepared for topics like current rates, instead of spending the week on bookshelves and cricket videos.

qa.q: How does Sabina see what happened to Bhupen?
qa.a: Sabina thinks he never gave himself a chance, because his certainty of failing kept him from preparing, but Sabina chooses kindness and makes him tea instead of saying it.

grounding: A flatmate watches a young man who expects to fail a bank interview avoid preparation, arrive rattled and blank, then call it proof.

passage:
Monday: Tenzin's second week at the Delhi office. At the tea counter the familiar thought came: they've already formed their groups, I'll be invisible. He noticed it this time, the way you notice a song stuck in your head. So he spoke first. 'Binita, is that a money plant on your desk? Mine keeps dying.' She laughed and gave him two tips.
Thursday: the team meeting. His forecast said he'd stumble, so he prepared his three slides the night before and practised once aloud. It went mostly fine. Someone asked about costs and he didn't know. He wrote it down instead of shrinking.
Next Tuesday: Binita waved him over to lunch. He counted quietly: two warm conversations, one question he couldn't answer, zero people ignoring him. Not bad evidence. That afternoon the intern turned in a weak draft. Tenzin didn't write her off; he sent it back with clear notes and said, 'I think you can make this sharp by Friday.'

qa.q: What did Tenzin ask Binita on Monday?
qa.a: He asked, 'Binita, is that a money plant on your desk? Mine keeps dying.'

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel about the question he couldn't answer on Thursday?
qa.a: He seemed steady rather than crushed; he wrote it down instead of shrinking, treating it as something to fix, not proof of failure.

qa.q: Which small choices helped Tenzin break his forecast, and why did they work?
qa.a: Speaking first at the tea counter and preparing his slides the night before gave people a chance to respond warmly, which gave him new evidence.

qa.q: How might the intern feel after reading Tenzin's notes?
qa.a: The intern would likely feel taken seriously, since Tenzin said she could make it sharp by Friday instead of writing her off.

grounding: Shows a young man noticing his forecast of being ignored, acting against it in small ways, counting results as new evidence and holding an intern to a high but fair standard.

passage: Sit, Vaibhav. My own nephew, starting a new job on Monday and already saying they won't like you. Your Indu Masi said the same thing in 1996, at the mill office in Surat. I was twenty-four, the only woman in accounts, and I was sure the manager thought I couldn't do the ledgers. One night I caught myself practising excuses in the mirror. Excuses, before anything had happened! So I did the opposite. I checked the ledger twice and on Monday I spoke first in the meeting. The manager asked three hard questions. I answered two. The third I wrote in my diary and brought back the next day. Two out of three, beta. That was new information, not a verdict. Years later, when I ran that office, I gave my juniors the full ledger, not the easy half, and sat with them till they could do it. So. What small thing will you do first on Monday?

qa.q: How many of the manager's questions did Indu Masi answer in that first meeting?
qa.a: Indu Masi answered two of the three, and wrote the third in the diary and brought it back the next day.

qa.q: What was Indu Masi feeling on catching the excuses being practised in the mirror?
qa.a: Indu Masi was afraid the manager doubted the ledger work, and seeing those excuses showed that the fear was running ahead of the facts.

qa.q: What small first step could Vaibhav take on Monday, based on the story?
qa.a: Vaibhav could pick one thing to do early, like preparing well for the first task or speaking first to a colleague, and then look at how people actually respond.

qa.q: How might Indu Masi's juniors have felt about getting the full ledger?
qa.a: They may have been nervous at first but also trusted, since Indu Masi expected real work from them and sat with them till they could do it.

grounding: Indu Masi tells Vaibhav about once noticing a fearful forecast, acting against it by preparing and speaking first, reading the result as evidence and later holding juniors to high, fair standards.

passage: The sangeet was in a marriage lawn outside Lucknow, and Divyansh knew exactly one person there: the groom, Mohit, who was being pulled in six directions. The music was so loud that conversation meant shouting. Divyansh felt the old prediction settle in: I'll stand by the wall all night and leave early. He noticed it and decided to test it. First, the uncle at the chai stall. 'Is this the ginger one?' They talked about trains for ten minutes. Then the lights died in a power cut, and in the dark he helped Mohit's cousins drag chairs away from the dance floor. He'd assumed they would be snobbish; he gave them the same fair chance he wanted for himself. One cousin shared her phone torch and asked how he knew Mohit. When the power came back, he did his count: three good conversations, one that went nowhere. Not the lonely night he'd forecast.

qa.q: What did Divyansh ask the uncle at the chai stall?
qa.a: He asked, 'Is this the ginger one?'

qa.q: What was Divyansh expecting when he first arrived at the sangeet?
qa.a: He expected to stand by the wall all night and leave early, since he knew only Mohit, who was busy.

qa.q: How did the power cut become a turning point for Divyansh?
qa.a: Instead of hiding in the dark, he chose to help Mohit's cousins move chairs, which led to a real conversation with one of them.

qa.q: If you were one of Mohit's cousins, how might you have seen Divyansh that night?
qa.a: You would probably see a friendly, helpful guest rather than a stranger by the wall, which made it easy to share a torch and chat.

grounding: A young man notices his forecast of a lonely evening, acts against it in small steps despite noise and a power cut, and counts the results as fresh evidence.

passage: Rain was leaking through the classroom roof, so Miss had to hand back the maths tests from the one dry corner. Amandeep's paper had a wet blotch next to the red 9 out of 25. Jatin's was also a 9. Walking home under Jatin's small umbrella, their shoulders getting soaked, Amandeep kicked a puddle. 'I'm stupid. I'm always going to be stupid at maths.' Jatin was quiet for a bit. 'I didn't study that chapter,' he said. 'The fractions one. I was doing cricket all week.' At the gate, Jatin asked, 'Want to do fractions at my house tomorrow?' Amandeep shook his head. 'What's the use?' That evening Jatin sat under a dripping balcony with his book open. Amandeep folded his test into a tiny square and pushed it deep into his bag.

qa.q: What marks did both boys get on the maths test?
qa.a: Amandeep's paper had a red 9 out of 25, and Jatin's was also a 9.

qa.q: How can you tell Amandeep felt hopeless about maths?
qa.a: He said 'I'm always going to be stupid at maths', shook his head at Jatin's offer, and folded his test into a tiny square.

qa.q: What could Amandeep try the next time he gets a low mark?
qa.a: He could ask which chapter he didn't understand, like Jatin did, and join Jatin to practise fractions instead of saying 'What's the use?'

qa.q: How might Jatin feel when Amandeep says no to studying together?
qa.a: Jatin may feel a little disappointed, since he wanted to try again together and Amandeep has given up before starting.

grounding: Two boys with the same low mark explain it differently: one calls himself stupid for good and stops trying, the other blames an unstudied chapter and studies again.

passage: On the stairs of Building C, in their Mumbai colony, Farida and Nandini compared their Hindi test papers. Both had 11 out of 30. Nandini pointed at the red circles. 'I didn't study the poem chapter. I thought it wouldn't come.' Farida pulled her knees up. 'I'm stupid,' she said. 'I'm stupid in Hindi and I'll always be stupid in Hindi.' A pigeon landed on the railing and they both watched it. 'You got the grammar right,' Nandini said. 'So?' The next evening Nandini's Nani made her read the poem aloud three times on the same stairs. Farida walked past with her cycle and didn't stop. When Nandini called out, 'Come, we'll learn it together!' Farida just rang her bell and kept going.

qa.q: What marks did Farida and Nandini get in the Hindi test?
qa.a: Both had 11 out of 30.

qa.q: What does Farida pulling her knees up and saying 'I'm stupid' suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels ashamed and sure the problem is permanent, so there is no point trying.

qa.q: What could help Farida the next evening on the stairs?
qa.a: She could stop her cycle and learn the poem with Nandini, starting from the grammar she already got right.

qa.q: What is it like for Nandini when Farida rides past?
qa.a: Nandini wants to help Farida and learn together, so it may feel lonely and a bit worrying when Farida just rings her bell and keeps going.

grounding: Two girls get the same low mark; one says she is stupid and gives up, the other blames a skipped chapter and practises it.

passage:
'Chacha, don't look at my report card. I'm stupid.'
'Jatin, it's one test.'
'It's science. I'm stupid in science. I'll always be.'
'Hm. Gunjan, what did you get?'
'Same marks,' said Gunjan, not looking up from her rice. 'Twelve.'
'And are you stupid too?'
'No! I didn't study the magnets chapter. I spent the whole week on my dance practice.'
'So what happens next?'
'I'll do magnets on Sunday. Ramesh Chacha, will you check me?'
'If you let me eat first.'
Jatin pushed his dal around. 'She's just lucky.'
'Lucky with twelve?' said Ramesh Chacha. 'Jatin, which part did you get wrong?'
'All of it.'
'All of it? Let's see.'
Jatin didn't move. After dinner Gunjan spread her book on the floor. Jatin went to his room and shut the door.

qa.q: Which chapter did Gunjan say she didn't study?
qa.a: Gunjan said she didn't study the magnets chapter.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when he said 'She's just lucky'?
qa.a: He seemed discouraged and defensive, as if Gunjan's plan made his own giving up feel worse, so he explained her calm as luck.

qa.q: What small step could Jatin take after dinner?
qa.a: He could show Ramesh Chacha the test so they can find the specific parts he got wrong, instead of deciding it was all of it.

qa.q: How does Ramesh Chacha see Jatin's words 'All of it'?
qa.a: Ramesh Chacha doesn't accept that it is all wrong and wants to check the paper, seeing the problem as something specific and fixable.

grounding: Two children with the same low science mark explain it differently at dinner, one as being stupid and one as an unstudied chapter, and only the second plans to try again.

passage:
Monday: Rekha dropped an easy catch at cricket practice. Walking off, she muttered to Charu, 'I ruin everything. I'm useless at all of it.' That night she didn't open her maths homework. What was the point?
Wednesday: the maths test came back with a C. 'See? I'm dumb at everything,' Rekha said at the water cooler. Charu frowned. 'You got a B last month. And you didn't do Monday's homework.' That evening Rekha wrote 'Things I'm bad at' in her rough book: catching, maths, speaking in class. Writing it down felt honest, like facing facts.
Saturday: the science club was building its water rocket at ten. Rekha had been excited about it for a month. At nine she messaged Charu: 'Not going. I'll just mess it up like everything else.' Charu replied, 'You designed the fins!' Rekha put the phone face down on the bed and stared at the ceiling fan.

qa.q: What happened to Rekha at cricket practice on Monday?
qa.a: Rekha dropped an easy catch at cricket practice.

qa.q: Why did writing the 'Things I'm bad at' list feel honest to Rekha?
qa.a: She felt defeated and believed one dropped catch and one C proved she was bad at everything, so the list seemed like plain facts rather than a gloomy habit.

qa.q: Where was the turning point for Rekha, and what could she have done?
qa.a: On Saturday she could have gone to the rocket build anyway, testing her belief against the fact that she designed the fins.

qa.q: How might Charu feel reading 'Not going'?
qa.a: Charu probably felt frustrated and worried, because Charu could see Rekha giving up on something Rekha had been excited about for a month.

grounding: A teenage girl treats one setback as proof she fails at everything, skips homework and a science-club build, while treating this as facing facts.

passage: Trisha, you think I was always this cheerful old man? At sixteen your Ojas Dadu was the gloomiest boy in Nagpur. When I failed the chemistry practical, I told myself, you are finished, you are a fool at everything. And I believed it completely. The drawing competition that month, I didn't enter. The school cricket selection, I didn't go. My friends said, 'Arre, it was one practical.' I said, 'You don't understand, I'm just being honest about myself.' It felt like honesty. It felt grown up. Only much later I noticed that my father spoke the same way. When his scooter broke, it was 'our family never has luck'. When it rained on a holiday, 'this always happens to us'. I had learned that voice like I learned his walk. So when you say, 'I'm bad at everything', beti, I listen carefully. Whose voice is that?

qa.q: What did Ojas Dadu fail at sixteen?
qa.a: He failed the chemistry practical.

qa.q: What did young Ojas believe after failing, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He believed he was finished and a fool at everything, which shows in how he skipped both the drawing competition and the cricket selection.

qa.q: What could Trisha do the next time she hears herself say 'I'm bad at everything'?
qa.a: She could stop and ask whose voice that is, as Dadu suggests, and look at the one real setback instead of giving up on everything.

qa.q: How might Ojas's friends have seen him skipping the drawing competition and cricket selection?
qa.a: They probably saw a boy giving up on things he could do because of one failed practical, which is why they said it was only one practical.

grounding: A grandfather tells his granddaughter how, as a teenager, he saw one failure as proof he was bad at everything and gave up, a habit he later realised he had learned from his father.

passage: The monsoon arrived a day early on the school camp near Lonavala. At four in the afternoon, Ganga's tent sagged and collapsed in the rain, soaking her sleeping bag. The others shrieked and laughed and ran for the dining shed. Ganga stood in the mud. 'Of course,' she said. 'I mess up everything. Even tents.' Farhan held up a snapped pole. 'Ganga, this was broken. Nobody could have kept it up.' She didn't look at it. 'It's always me. I'll be useless on the trek tomorrow too. I'm staying back.' 'It's the easy trail,' Farhan said. 'You'll slow everyone down.' At dinner she ate quietly, already sure. In the morning, when the teacher called names for the trek, Ganga said she had a headache. Farhan watched her from the gate as the group left without her.

qa.q: What did Farhan hold up after the tent collapsed?
qa.a: Farhan held up a snapped pole.

qa.q: Why didn't Ganga look at the broken pole Farhan held up?
qa.a: She was already sure the fault was hers and would always be, so she didn't want evidence that pointed to something else.

qa.q: What choice could Ganga have made in the morning?
qa.a: She could have gone on the easy trail and seen how the trek actually went, instead of saying she had a headache and staying back.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel watching the group leave without Ganga?
qa.a: Farhan may feel sad and a bit helpless, since Farhan tried to show her the pole was broken and she still gave up.

grounding: A teenage girl blames herself for a tent failure caused by a broken pole, decides she'll fail at the trek too and gives up without trying.

passage:
Lalit,
Thermodynamics came back: 31. Failed. My first reaction was the usual one: I'm not engineering material, I've been fooling everyone. I spent Sunday lying on my bed believing it.
Then I did the thing you once did for me. I got a paper and wrote down the facts. Passed the other four subjects, two with good marks. Lost almost all the thermo marks on the long numerical from Unit 4, which I skipped in revision because I had viral fever that week. The short questions were mostly fine.
So the evidence says: one unit, one bad week. Not 'fooling everyone'.
I'm still annoyed. I'm not pretending this is great. But I've made one change. From Monday, I'm solving one past paper every Saturday with the study group, timed, starting with Unit 4.
Reply when you're free. And thanks, even though you don't know you helped.
Chaitanya

qa.q: Which part of the exam did Chaitanya lose most marks on?
qa.a: Chaitanya lost almost all the thermo marks on the long numerical from Unit 4.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel on Sunday, and what changed that?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt like a fraud who wasn't engineering material, until writing down the facts showed the problem was one unit and one bad week.

qa.q: Which step in Chaitanya's letter turned the failure into a plan?
qa.a: Checking the actual evidence and naming one change, a timed past paper every Saturday starting with Unit 4, turned the harsh story into something to act on.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel reading that Lalit helped without knowing it?
qa.a: Lalit would probably feel touched and glad that something Lalit once did for Chaitanya was remembered and used.

grounding: A student who failed an exam writes to Lalit about checking the harsh story against facts, finding other causes and choosing one change, without pretending to be cheerful.

passage: Sarika, you asked how I stayed sane after failing stats. Okay, so, I'm Lavanya, second-year psych, and the funny part is we'd literally studied explanatory style that semester. Didn't stop my brain. The result came, 38, and my head went: you're stupid, you'll never do research, everyone knew but you. I cried in the library washroom, honestly. Then that night I thought, fine, I'd tell a client to check the evidence, so check it. I opened the paper. Lost marks on regression, all of them, and I'd missed both regression classes for my cousin's wedding. The descriptive stats section? Full marks. So, other explanation: not 'stupid', just two missed classes. And one change: I booked the professor's office hours for Tuesday and asked for the regression notes. I wasn't happy, Sarika. I was still upset. But I was upset about something real and small, not something huge and made up.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya miss both regression classes?
qa.a: Lavanya missed both regression classes for a cousin's wedding.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling right after the result came?
qa.a: Lavanya felt crushed and ashamed, with thoughts like 'you're stupid' and 'you'll never do research', and cried in the library washroom.

qa.q: What would you advise Sarika to take from Lavanya's approach if Sarika fails an exam?
qa.a: Look at the actual paper to see where the marks were lost, find the real cause and choose one step, like booking office hours, instead of believing the harsh first story.

qa.q: How might the professor see Lavanya coming to office hours for regression notes?
qa.a: The professor would likely see a student taking the failure seriously and working on a specific gap, not someone who has given up.

grounding: A psychology student describes disputing their inner critic after failing, checking where marks were lost, finding a smaller explanation and making one change while still feeling upset.

passage: I'm Ramesh, and I share a table with Yamini in the hostel reading room. The day the nursing pharmacology results came out, she failed by four marks. I saw her go very still, then put her head on her arms for a long time. I don't know everything she was thinking. I know she said, almost to herself, 'I'm going to be a terrible nurse.' An hour later she was drawing two columns in her notebook. From across the table I could read the headings: 'What I'm telling myself' and 'What the paper shows'. She kept flipping between the result sheet and the question paper. At one point she said, 'Drug interactions. Only drug interactions. Everything else passed.' Then she circled something and wrote 'flashcards, 15 min daily'. She didn't smile or say she was fine. She just packed her bag differently the next morning, with a stack of blank cards on top.

qa.q: How many marks did Yamini fail by?
qa.a: She failed by four marks.

qa.q: What did Yamini seem to be feeling right after the result, according to Ramesh?
qa.a: She seemed shocked and discouraged; she went very still, put her head on her arms, and said, 'I'm going to be a terrible nurse.'

qa.q: Which choice turned Yamini's night around?
qa.a: Drawing two columns to compare what she was telling herself with what the paper shows helped her find that only drug interactions went wrong and pick one step, daily flashcards.

qa.q: What might it be like for Ramesh to watch Yamini go from head-down to drawing columns?
qa.a: Ramesh may have felt worried seeing Yamini so still, then relieved and quietly impressed to watch the bad result turn into a plan without any pretending to be fine.

grounding: A hostel mate watches a student who failed an exam compare her harsh thoughts with the evidence, find the real gap and choose one change without false cheer.

passage:
Monday, three weeks before the Jaipur wedding: at the planning meeting, Zainab watched her two colleagues. Kunal waved off the list of risks. 'Everything will be fine, it's a wedding, not a war.' Aditi kept writing. 'The tent supplier was late last season. I'm calling a backup today, just in case.'
Thursday, ten days later: the tent supplier phoned to say half the canopies were stuck in a warehouse. Kunal shrugged. 'They'll sort it out.' Aditi was already on the phone to her backup, confirming a delivery date. 'I think we can still pull this off,' she said to Zainab. 'If we move now.'
Saturday, the mehendi evening: Aditi's side of the lawn was covered and lit. Kunal was running between guests with plastic sheets as a light drizzle started. Later, over cold coffee, Zainab noticed that Aditi hadn't been the gloomy one at all. She'd been the one who actually believed things could go well.

qa.q: What did Kunal say while waving off the list of risks?
qa.a: Kunal said, 'Everything will be fine, it's a wedding, not a war.'

qa.q: What did Zainab realise about Aditi after the mehendi evening?
qa.a: Zainab realised Aditi hadn't been gloomy at all; Aditi was the one who actually believed things could go well and planned for it.

qa.q: Which choice made the difference when the supplier phoned on Thursday?
qa.a: Aditi had already lined up a backup on Monday, so she could confirm a new delivery date at once instead of hoping it would sort itself out.

qa.q: What was the mehendi evening like for Kunal?
qa.a: Kunal was stuck running between guests with plastic sheets in the drizzle, likely stressed and embarrassed that Kunal's reassurance hadn't protected anyone.

grounding: A wedding planner watches one colleague insist all will be fine and ignore risks while another hopes and prepares, and sees that real optimism is the second kind.

passage: Mehak, come, sit. People in this office laugh that old Sonali checks the drainage before every monsoon. Here's why. In 1994 I was twenty-five, a sub-editor at a newspaper press in Kolkata. Two men ran the printing floor then. One, Bose babu, used to say, 'Nothing will happen, the rains always pass.' The other, young Tapan, spent a week lifting the paper rolls onto wooden pallets and clearing the drain behind the machines. People teased him. 'Pessimist!' I thought so too, a little. That August the water came in knee-deep. Bose babu's store room lost two weeks of paper. Tapan's rolls were dry. And here's what I noticed: Tapan wasn't gloomy. He was the only one smiling while we bailed water, saying, 'We'll be printing by Thursday.' And we were. So when you tell me everything will be fine, Mehak, I believe you. Just show me the plan too. That's the kind of hope that works.

qa.q: What did Tapan do to prepare for the rains?
qa.a: Tapan spent a week lifting the paper rolls onto wooden pallets and clearing the drain behind the machines.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel about Tapan when people teased him, and how did that change?
qa.a: Sonali thought a little that he was a pessimist, but after the flood saw he was the hopeful one, smiling and saying they'd be printing by Thursday.

qa.q: What could Mehak do the next time Mehak says 'everything will be fine'?
qa.a: Mehak could back that confidence with a clear plan for what could go wrong, the way Tapan cleared the drain and raised the rolls.

qa.q: How might Bose babu have felt when his store room lost two weeks of paper?
qa.a: He may have felt shocked and regretful, since his easy belief that the rains always pass left the paper unprotected.

grounding: A senior tells a junior colleague how they once watched one man ignore flood risks with cheerful words and another prepare while staying hopeful, showing hope joined with planning.

passage: Their food truck in Toronto had three weeks of rent left and sales were down with the first snow. Simran, who handled the accounts, sat in the cold cab and listened to her two partners. Deepak stamped his boots. 'Relax. Everything will be fine. People always want hot food in winter.' He wanted to order the usual amount of stock. Rekha had a notebook open. 'Sales fell a third since November. If we keep ordering the same, we waste money. But I think we can make it.' She suggested a smaller menu, a soup special, and parking near the hospital at night-shift change. Deepak rolled his eyes. 'You always see problems.' Simran looked from one to the other. Deepak sounded hopeful but had no plan. Rekha sounded worried but was the only one planning to win. Simran picked up her pen and started pricing the soup.

qa.q: How many weeks of rent did the food truck have left?
qa.a: The truck had three weeks of rent left.

qa.q: What did Simran realise while listening to her partners?
qa.a: Simran realised that Deepak sounded hopeful but had no plan, while Rekha sounded worried yet was the only one planning to win.

qa.q: Which choice did Simran make at the end, and why does it fit the situation?
qa.a: Simran started pricing the soup, backing Rekha's plan because it faces the falling sales while still aiming to succeed.

qa.q: How might Rekha feel when Deepak says 'You always see problems'?
qa.a: Rekha might feel frustrated and misunderstood, since she is trying to save the business, not predict its failure.

grounding: A partner watches another partner insist all will be fine while ignoring falling sales, and another combine hope with a practical plan, in a truck short on money.

passage: Beta, sit. You're worried about your friend, so let me tell you about Wasim. I'm your Suraj Chacha; you know he was my closest friend. In 1998 the floods ruined his cloth shop in Bhagalpur. He was twenty-four. He sat on my verandah and said, 'It's over, Suraj. I'm finished.' I wanted to say, 'Don't talk like that.' But I didn't. I let him talk for an hour. He talked about the stock, his father's name on the board, his fear of facing the lenders. When he was quiet, I took a notebook. 'What can't we change?' The stock was gone. The season was lost. 'And what can?' He knew the weavers. He had customers who trusted him. 'One thing for tomorrow,' I said. He chose: visit the weaver in Nathnagar. That's all. He didn't cheer up that day. But he went. You can't order a man to hope, beta. You can only walk beside him.

qa.q: What happened to Wasim's shop in 1998?
qa.a: The floods ruined his cloth shop in Bhagalpur.

qa.q: Why did Suraj Chacha hold back from saying 'Don't talk like that'?
qa.a: He wanted Wasim to feel heard, so he chose to listen for an hour rather than brush aside Wasim's despair.

qa.q: Which turning point helped Wasim move, and what can the listener learn for their own friend?
qa.a: Splitting what couldn't change from what could, and then choosing one thing for tomorrow, gave Wasim a real step; the listener could do the same after first listening.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt being allowed to talk for an hour?
qa.a: Wasim may have felt heard and less alone, which made it easier to think about what he could still do.

grounding: An uncle recalls listening fully to a despairing friend, separating what was fixed from what could change and helping him pick one small step.

passage: The power went off in Harish's Chennai flat just as Parul arrived, and the fan slowed to a stop in the thick heat. By the light of Parul's phone, at eleven percent battery, Harish said the export order was cancelled. His biggest buyer, gone. 'Two years of work. I'm not cut out for business.' Parul sat on the floor beside him and didn't say it would be okay. 'Tell me what happened.' Harish talked about the buyer's email, the unpaid weavers, his mother asking questions. Parul listened, sweat running down both their faces. Then, before the phone died: 'What's fixed?' 'The order's gone. The money's gone.' 'What isn't?' He thought. 'I still have the samples. The weavers still trust me.' 'One step, tomorrow.' 'Send the samples to that shop in Bengaluru that asked last year.' The screen went black. Harish laughed a little in the dark. 'Okay. One step.'

qa.q: What did Harish say about the export order?
qa.a: Harish said the export order was cancelled and his biggest buyer was gone.

qa.q: What does Harish's small laugh in the dark suggest about how he felt by the end?
qa.a: It suggests some of the heaviness had lifted and he felt a little hope, now that he had one clear step.

qa.q: What did Parul do instead of saying it would be okay, and why did it work?
qa.a: Parul asked Harish to tell what happened and listened first, then helped him sort what was fixed from what wasn't, so the step came from Harish himself.

qa.q: How might the weavers be affected if Harish follows through on the Bengaluru samples?
qa.a: The weavers, who still trust him and haven't been paid, could get new work and payment again if the samples lead to an order.

grounding: A young adult listens to Harish's despair in a hot power cut without dismissing it, then helps sort what is fixed from what can change and find one next step.

passage: On the terrace of their Hyderabad building, Shankar sat with his back to the water tank. 'The restaurant shut. Three years of training. I'll never cook in a real kitchen again.' Madhav passed him a steel glass of chai and didn't answer right away. Below, a pressure cooker whistled in someone's flat. 'That sounds awful,' Madhav said finally. 'Three years.' Shankar talked about the owner's debts, the last service, the dishwasher who cried. Madhav just nodded. After a while he asked, 'Okay. Which parts can't you change?' 'The restaurant's gone. I can't get it back.' 'And which parts can you?' Shankar turned the glass. 'My skills. Chef Anand liked my work.' 'So one thing, today?' 'Message Chef Anand for a reference.' Madhav held out Shankar's phone. Shankar laughed, took it, and started typing.

qa.q: Where did Shankar sit on the terrace?
qa.a: Shankar sat with his back to the water tank.

qa.q: How can you tell Shankar felt hopeless at the start?
qa.a: He said he would never cook in a real kitchen again after three years of training, speaking as if the loss was permanent.

qa.q: Which moment turned the conversation, and why did it help?
qa.a: When Madhav asked which parts Shankar could change, Shankar remembered his skills and Chef Anand, and picked one step he could take today.

qa.q: What would change if Madhav had said 'Cheer up, you'll find something' at the start?
qa.a: Shankar might have felt brushed off and stopped talking, and they might never have reached the idea of messaging Chef Anand.

grounding: A young man listens to Shankar's despair after the restaurant closes, acknowledges it, then helps separate the fixed from the changeable and take one small step.

passage:
'Arre, why is Noor crying?'
'Her balloon popped, Rajni. Look at her.'
'Oh no. Come, Noor, come to me.'
'Rajni, look at Jassi now.'
'Jassi? Why are you crying, baby? Your balloon is fine!'
Jasleen, two, held her red balloon tight. Her lip wobbled, then she wailed too, looking at Noor.
'Nothing happened to you, Jassi.'
'She heard Noor,' said Bebe. 'Babies catch it like yawns. Pick her up.'

qa.q: What happened to Noor's balloon?
qa.a: Noor's balloon popped.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen start to cry even though her balloon was fine?
qa.a: She was upset by hearing and seeing Noor cry, so she felt the sadness too without knowing why.

qa.q: What could Rajni do to help Jasleen right then?
qa.a: Rajni could pick Jasleen up as Bebe said and hold her close so she feels safe again.

qa.q: How does Bebe explain Jasleen's tears?
qa.a: Bebe sees it as natural: Jasleen heard Noor, and babies catch crying like yawns.

grounding: Shows a two-year-old at a family gathering who starts crying on hearing another toddler cry, without any reason of her own.

passage:
Note from Nilesh, room teacher, Little Steps nursery, Tuesday:
At drop-off, Mia cried hard when her dad left. Tarun was stacking blocks happily nearby. He stopped, stared at Mia, and his face crumpled. Soon he was crying too, then two more children. None of them had any reason of their own. I sat on the mat, picked up Mia, and hummed our bus song. Tarun crawled over and leaned on my knee. Within a few minutes the room was quiet again 🙂

qa.q: What was Tarun doing before Mia started crying?
qa.a: Tarun was stacking blocks happily nearby.

qa.q: What does Tarun's face crumpling as he stared at Mia suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Mia's crying upset him and he began to feel the same distress, even though nothing had happened to him.

qa.q: How did Nilesh help the room calm down, and why did it work?
qa.a: Nilesh sat on the mat, held Mia and hummed the bus song, which calmed Mia and drew Tarun in, so the calm spread like the crying had.

qa.q: What was drop-off like for the other children in the room?
qa.a: Two more children started crying too, so for them it was a sudden sad moment that none of them could explain.

grounding: A nursery teacher's note records how one toddler's crying spread to others who had no reason of their own.

passage: At the anganwadi in the village, the children sat on a mat eating chana. Suddenly a goat bleated loudly at the door and little Faiz burst into tears. Dilnaz, two, stopped chewing. She looked at Faiz. Her eyes went wide and her chin began to shake. Then she was crying too, and so was the boy beside her. Zeenat didi laughed softly, pulled all three onto her lap and sang the rain song until the sobbing stopped.

qa.q: What made Faiz burst into tears?
qa.a: A goat bleated loudly at the door.

qa.q: How can you tell Dilnaz was starting to feel upset?
qa.a: She stopped chewing, her eyes went wide and her chin began to shake as she looked at Faiz.

qa.q: What did Zeenat didi do well to calm the children?
qa.a: She pulled all three onto her lap and sang the rain song, giving them comfort together instead of scolding.

qa.q: Why might the boy beside Dilnaz have started crying?
qa.a: He probably caught the sadness from Faiz and Dilnaz crying next to him, not because of anything that happened to him.

grounding: Shows toddlers at a village anganwadi catching crying from one another after one child is startled.
